implementation_notes: The C++ default is a small header of generic combiners: lambdas and `std::function<Sig>` make callables first-class, `std::invoke` handles member pointers, and variadic templates let `and_then(f, g)` return a new lambda with no virtual dispatch, replacing the class hierarchy of Command/Strategy objects the pattern removes. Keep the combiners as templates where they are hot: `std::function` type-erases and may heap-allocate the target, which is exactly what you want only when a combinator must be stored polymorphically, passed across a stable ABI, or collected in one container.
pitfalls: `std::function` copies the target and may allocate: a chain built from `std::function` values pays an indirect call and possible heap traffic per step.
A lambda that captures by reference and outlives the scope produces a dangling callable; anything handed to another thread or stored in the DSL must capture by value.
Template combiners instantiate per callable type, so long chains bloat compile time and turn one type error into pages of instantiation backtrace.

variants.name: C++20 range adaptor closures piped with operator|
variants.implementation_notes: In C++20 the combinator DSL is in the standard library: range adaptor closure objects compose with `operator|` (`r | std::views::transform(f) | std::views::filter(p)`), and a user type opts in by deriving from `std::ranges::range_adaptor_closure<D>` so its own combiners chain the same way. Choose this when the domain is 'elements of a sequence': composition is a value you can name, evaluation stays lazy, and the combiners are standard and optimised. For non-sequence domains (plain `A -> B` composition) the template combiners of the default variant remain the right tool.
pitfalls: Adaptor closures store copies of their callables: capturing `this` or a reference inside a view that outlives the object is a dangling reference, and a view over a temporary range is always dangling.
Laziness caches nothing: iterating the same composed view twice re-runs the whole pipeline, and stateful or side-effecting callables behave accordingly.
Chaining with `|` requires the left operand to be a range or an adaptor closure; mixing a plain callable into the pipe silently fails overload resolution with a wall of concept diagnostics.

variants.name: Boost.Spirit: EBNF grammar as an expression-template DSEL
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Spirit is the pattern's classic C++ home: overloaded operators (`>>` for sequencing, `|` for alternatives, prefix `*`/`+` for repetition), expression templates and template metaprogramming build a recursive-descent parser whose grammar is executable C++ in EBNF-like notation, with no code-generation step. Choose it for micro-parsers inside a C++-only build where a separate lex/yacc toolchain would be overkill; the price is compile time and template error diagnostics, which is why projects that only need sequence adaptors should take the ranges variant instead.
pitfalls: Spirit grammars are types: a rule used before assignment, or a stray non-parser expression in the chain, produces error messages measured in pages.
Attribute propagation (what each combinator binds, and how tuples nest) is the real learning curve; getting it wrong yields grammars that compile and mis-parse.
Compile time and object-code size grow sharply with grammar depth - keep each grammar in its own translation unit and prefer `qi::rule` over inline `auto` grammars.
